subject: Coffee & Tea
title: How Leaves Are Picked
description: A micro-lesson that makes How Leaves Are Picked usable.

hook.text: The finest teas use only the bud and top two leaves of each branch—called the 'flush.'

buildup.text: Hand-picking selects only these young tips. It's slow, expensive, and produces the best quality.

discovery.text: Machine harvesting is fast but indiscriminate—older, tougher leaves get mixed in, lowering quality.

twist.text: Some premium teas use only the unopened bud. Silver Needle white tea is just furry, pale buds.

climax.text: Picking standard defines quality ceiling. No processing technique can make a coarse leaf taste delicate.

punchline.text: Two leaves and a bud. Quality starts at the tip.

quiz.question: What is the ideal tea 'flush' for premium teas?
options: The bud and top two leaves

details.summary: Tea quality begins with the pluck. The finest teas use only the bud and top two leaves, hand-picked in early spring. Machine harvesting cuts costs but includes stems and older leaves, reducing quality. Picking standard, timing, and altitude all profoundly affect the final cup.
details.whyItMatters: The plucking standard determines the tea's potential before any processing begins. Spring buds command premium prices because of their concentrated flavor compounds.
takeaways: The bud and top two leaves produce the highest quality tea
Hand-picking preserves leaf integrity for premium teas
Spring harvests yield the most prized and expensive teas

faq.question: Why are spring teas more expensive than summer teas?
faq.answer: After winter dormancy, tea bushes accumulate amino acids and flavor compounds in their buds. The first spring flush produces leaves with concentrated sweetness and complexity. Summer growth is faster, diluting these compounds, so summer teas are less nuanced and cheaper.

faq.question: How much tea can one picker harvest per day?
faq.answer: An experienced hand picker harvests about 20 to 30 kilograms of fresh leaves per day, which yields roughly 5 kilograms of finished tea. Machine harvesting collects far more but cannot match the selectivity of hand-picking for premium grades.
